lesson.title: Why Connecting a Meter Changes What It Measures: The Loading Effect
lesson.summary: The loading effect is the voltage drop that appears whenever a finite load resistance is connected to a source with nonzero output resistance, and it becomes negligible only when the load resistance is much larger than the source's output resistance.
lesson.body:
The loading effect is what happens whenever any load, and a load here can mean a resistor, the next stage's input resistance, or a measuring instrument like a voltmeter, gets connected to a source that has some nonzero output resistance. The moment current is allowed to flow, it flows through the source's own R_out, and that current creates a voltage drop that quietly steals part of the signal before it ever reaches whatever is trying to measure or use it. Input resistance, output resistance, and load resistance are really just three names for the two resistors in the exact same voltage divider that produces this effect: V_delivered = V_source times R_load divided by (R_out plus R_load).

A useful rule of thumb follows directly from that formula: the loading effect is negligible when the load resistance is roughly ten to a hundred times larger than the source's output resistance, becomes clearly noticeable once the two are comparable, and becomes severe once the load resistance drops below the output resistance.

Consider the classic case of voltmeter loading. A circuit under test has a true open circuit voltage of 10V at a point with Thevenin, or output, resistance R_out = 10 kilo ohm. Measuring it with a good digital voltmeter whose input resistance is R_in = 1,000,000 ohm, the measured voltage is 10V times 1,000,000 divided by (10,000 plus 1,000,000), which is 10V times 1,000,000 divided by 1,010,000, or about 9.901V. That is roughly one percent low, a negligible loading effect for most purposes.

Now take the same measurement with a cheap analog meter whose input resistance is only R_in = 10 kilo ohm, equal to the circuit's own output resistance. The measured voltage becomes 10V times 10,000 divided by 20,000, which is exactly 5V, only half the true value. The meter is not broken and nothing in the circuit changed, the reading is simply wrong by fifty percent, purely because the meter's own input resistance was low enough to meaningfully load down the circuit it was trying to observe.

This is exactly why the input resistance and output resistance chapters matter as a pair rather than in isolation. Wanting a driving circuit's output resistance to be low, and a receiving circuit's or instrument's input resistance to be high, is the same design principle stated from two different sides of the same connection, and it is the general rule for minimizing the loading effect anywhere a load resistance gets attached, whether that load is a plain resistor, an amplifier's next stage, or a meter probe someone just touched to a circuit.

The same arithmetic explains why an oscilloscope probe is usually specified with an input resistance of 1 megohm or more, and why a well designed amplifier is specified with an output resistance of a few ohms to a few hundred ohms rather than kilohms. Neither number is arbitrary, both exist to keep the ratio between them large enough that whatever gets connected to a circuit reveals what that circuit was already doing, rather than changing it. Once you can compute V_delivered from R_out and R_load directly, the loading effect stops being a mysterious measurement quirk and becomes exactly what it is: one more application of the same voltage divider that has run through every chapter in this sequence.
